query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a nanohierarchical architecture with spatial composition undulation into the high‐entropy alloy by tailored processing will lower both the coefficient of friction and wear rate over a broad temperature range by enabling an adaptive friction interface that forms a protective glaze layer during wear.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a refractory or complex concentrated alloy in its as-cast or conventionally processed state) lacking engineered nanostructure.
generation.intervention: Tailor the alloy’s microstructure via a single processing step (such as controlled thermomechanical treatment or additive manufacturing parameter tuning) to induce nano-coupled grains with integrated nanoprecipitates leading to spatial composition undulation.
generation.conditions: Operating under sliding wear conditions from room temperature up to approximately 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation that promotes the formation of an in situ, dense, nanocrystalline glaze layer upon sliding wear.
generation.mechanism: The engineered nanostructure releases frictional stress in stages and activates multiple deformation pathways. Under sliding conditions, this structure facilitates the formation of an adaptive, low-shear glaze layer that minimizes adhesive, abrasive, and oxidative wear, thereby reducing both friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated alloys, the modified alloy is expected to exhibit a notably lower coefficient of friction and a substantially reduced wear rate across the service-temperature range. (The magnitude of improvement remains to be clarified with testing, but prior studies indicate that wear rate improvements can be on the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm.)
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy without the engineered nanohierarchical microstructure.
generation.boundary: The intervention should remain effective under typical sliding wear conditions across room temperature to ~800 °C; however, extreme dynamic conditions or environments lacking sufficient sliding activation to form the glaze layer may not yield the same benefits.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the tunability of the nanostructure formation process, the uniformity of the adaptive friction interface activation across all temperatures, and the scalability of the processing method in industrial applications.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one group processed with the intervention to induce nanohierarchical architecture (with composition undulation) and one group kept as the untreated baseline. Subject both groups to controlled sliding wear tests over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C. Perform detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM) before and after testing to identify the formation of the glaze layer.
measurements: Coefficient of friction at multiple temperatures using a standardized tribometer
Wear rate measurement via weight loss or profilometry
Microstructural analysis to verify the formation of nanohierarchical features and the adaptive glaze layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not consistently exhibit significantly lower friction coefficients and wear rates across the tested temperature range compared to the untreated samples, or if the expected adaptive glaze layer is absent or not uniformly formed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear.
